bibliography.abstract: Drawing on (auto)ethnographic fieldwork in Manchester, UK, this paper explores how encounters with graphic vegan street activism may be understood as aesthetic interventions that destabilize the common sense perception of animal (product) consumption. Engaging with literature in vegan geographies, encounter, affective post-foundational political geography and (an)aesthetics, I argue that such encounters may unsettle the ‘sensible’ order of animal consumption by exposing the contingencies and exclusions that sustain it. These moments, I suggest, might make alternative relations to nonhuman animals newly thinkable, speakable and sense-able. Yet these encounters may not always be transformative. Drawing on the concept of ‘strategic unfeeling’ and the distinction between noise and voice, I trace how graphic encounters may be anaesthetised as ‘noise’: through protective disengagement by individuals or absorbed into the sensory excesses of the high street. Providing an understanding of such encounters beyond success or failure, this paper contributes to vegan geographies and broader debates in social and cultural geography by tracing how hegemonic human-nonhuman animal relations may, or may not, be unsettled. It offers insights into the affective and aesthetic conditions shaping political (im)possibilities, processes and change, as they unfold in contingent, nonlinear and contested ways.
bibliography.title: The political potential of (extra)ordinary encounters with vegan street activism

en.caveats: The findings are based on qualitative, autoethnographic fieldwork in a single city, which may limit generalizability to different cultural or urban contexts.
en.what: Based on autoethnographic fieldwork in Manchester, UK, this study examines how public encounters with graphic vegan street activism function as aesthetic interventions. It analyzes how these street displays challenge conventional norms of animal product consumption, while also tracing how passersby neutralize these encounters as 'noise' through protective disengagement or by absorbing them into the sensory clutter of the commercial high street.
en.why: The research moves beyond binary measures of activist success or failure to show how hegemonic human-animal relations are contested in public space, revealing the specific affective and aesthetic mechanisms that either enable or block political transformation during everyday encounters.
